sources.entry: Scalable web architecture and distributed systems

summary.title: Scalable Web Architecture and Distributed Systems
summary.one_liner: You learn the core principles of large-scale web design (availability, performance, reliability, scalability, manageability, cost) and the building blocks used to meet them, illustrated with an image-hosting example.
keywords: how to design a system for millions of users
takeaways: Scalability, availability, reliability, performance, manageability and cost are the key principles that drive large web system design, and they often conflict.
Splitting a system into services with clear interfaces (SOA) lets each part scale and fail independently, e.g. separating image reads from writes.
Redundancy, failover and shared-nothing nodes remove single points of failure; vertical scaling adds resources to one machine while horizontal scaling adds nodes.
Partitioning (sharding) spreads data across servers but brings challenges with data locality and inconsistency/race conditions.
Caches (local, global or distributed), proxies, indexes and load balancers are the main tools for fast data access at scale.
summary.summary: The chapter, from the Architecture of Open-Source Applications book, opens by defining the key principles of large web systems: availability, performance, reliability, scalability, manageability and cost, and notes how they trade off against each other. It then uses a hypothetical Flickr-like image hosting service to walk through services, read/write separation, redundancy, vertical versus horizontal scaling, and partitioning, discussing data locality and race conditions. The final part moves to scaling data access, introducing caches (local, global and distributed), proxies, indexes and load balancers; the excerpt ends partway through the discussion of caching. The approach is conceptual and explanatory, with examples and rough performance comparisons rather than code.
